paragraphs: “And what about Alyosha and his opinion, which you were so desperately anxious to hear?” cried Madame Hohlakov. Her voice was sarcastic and angry.

“I haven’t forgotten that,” cried Katerina Ivanovna, stopping short. “And why are you so hostile at a moment like this?” she added, with warm and bitter reproach. “What I said, I say again. I must have his opinion. More than that, I must have his decision! Whatever he says, that’s what will be done. You see how eager I am to hear you, Alexey Fyodorovitch.... But what’s the matter?”
“I couldn’t have believed it. I can’t understand it!” Alyosha cried suddenly, in distress.
“What? What?”

“He’s going to Moscow, and you cry out that you’re glad. You said it on purpose! Then you start explaining that you’re not glad of that but sorry—sorry to lose a friend. But that was acting too—you were playing a part—as if you were in a theater!”
“In a theater? What? What do you mean?” exclaimed Katerina Ivanovna, deeply astonished, flushing crimson and frowning.

“You assure him you’re sorry to lose a friend in him, and yet you keep telling him to his face how fortunate it is that he’s going,” said Alyosha breathlessly. He was standing at the table and had not sat down.
“What are you talking about? I don’t understand.”

“I don’t understand myself.... It was as if I saw something in a flash ... I know I’m not saying it properly, but I’ll say it anyway,” Alyosha went on in the same shaking, broken voice. “What I see is that perhaps you don’t love Dmitri at all ... and never have, from the beginning.... And Dmitri has never loved you either ... and only respects you.... I really don’t know how I dare say all this, but somebody must tell the truth ... because nobody here will tell the truth.”
“What truth?” cried Katerina Ivanovna, with a hysterical edge in her voice.

“I’ll tell you,” Alyosha went on in desperate haste, as though he were jumping off the top of a house. “Call Dmitri; I’ll fetch him—and let him come here and take your hand, and take Ivan’s, and join your hands together. Because you’re torturing Ivan, simply because you love him—and you’re torturing him because you love Dmitri out of ‘self-laceration’—with an unreal love—because you’ve talked yourself into it.”
Alyosha broke off and fell silent.
“You ... you ... you’re a little religious idiot—that’s what you are!” Katerina Ivanovna snapped. Her face was white and her lips trembled with anger.
Ivan suddenly laughed and stood up. His hat was in his hand.

“You’re mistaken, my good Alyosha,” he said, with a look Alyosha had never seen on his face before—a look of youthful sincerity and strong, irresistibly frank feeling. “Katerina Ivanovna has never cared for me! She has known all along that I cared for her—though I never said a word to her about my love—she knew, but she didn’t care for me. I was never her friend either, not for a single moment; she’s too proud to need my friendship. She kept me at her side as a means of revenge. With me, and on me, she took revenge for all the insults she has been getting from Dmitri ever since they first met. Even that first meeting has rankled in her heart as an insult—that’s what her heart is like! She has talked to me about nothing but her love for him. I’m leaving now; but believe me, Katerina Ivanovna, you really do love him. And the more he insults you, the more you love him—that’s your ‘laceration.’ You love him just as he is; you love him for insulting you. If he reformed, you’d give him up at once and stop loving him. But you need him so that you can keep contemplating your heroic faithfulness and reproach him for his unfaithfulness. And it all comes from your pride. Oh, there’s a great deal of humiliation and self-abasement in it, but it all comes from pride.... I’m too young, and I’ve loved you too much. I know I shouldn’t say this, that it would be more dignified of me simply to leave, and less offensive for you. But I’m going far away, and I will never come back.... It’s for ever. I don’t want to sit next to a ‘laceration.’... But I don’t know how to speak now. I’ve said everything.... Good-by, Katerina Ivanovna; you can’t be angry with me, because I am punished a hundred times more severely than you, if only by the fact that I’ll never see you again. Good-by! I don’t want your hand. You have tortured me too deliberately for me to forgive you at this moment. I’ll forgive you later, but now I don’t want your hand. ‘Den Dank, Dame, begehr ich nicht,’” he added, with a forced smile, showing, however, that he could read Schiller, and had read him until he knew him by heart—which Alyosha would never have believed. He walked out of the room without saying good-by even to his hostess, Madame Hohlakov. Alyosha clasped his hands.

“Ivan!” he cried desperately after him. “Come back, Ivan! No, nothing will make him come back now!” he cried again, realizing it with regret. “But it’s my fault, my fault! I started it! Ivan spoke angrily, and wrongly. Unjustly and angrily. He must come back here, he must come back,” Alyosha kept exclaiming frantically.
Katerina Ivanovna suddenly went into the next room.
“You’ve done no harm. You behaved beautifully, like an angel,” Madame Hohlakov whispered quickly and ecstatically to Alyosha. “I’ll do everything I can to stop Ivan Fyodorovitch from going.”
Her face shone with delight, to Alyosha’s great distress, but Katerina Ivanovna suddenly came back. She had two hundred-rouble notes in her hand.

“I have a great favor to ask of you, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she began, speaking to Alyosha in a seemingly calm and even voice, as though nothing had happened. “A week ago—yes, I think it was a week—Dmitri Fyodorovitch committed a hasty and unjust act—a very ugly act. There is a low tavern here, and in it he met that discharged officer, that captain, whom your father used to employ in some business. Dmitri Fyodorovitch somehow lost his temper with this captain, seized him by the beard and dragged him out into the street, and for some distance along it, in that insulting way. And I’m told that the captain’s son, a boy, hardly more than a child, who goes to school here, saw it and ran beside them, crying and begging for his father, appealing to everyone to defend him, while everyone laughed. You must forgive me, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I can’t think of that disgraceful act of _his_ without indignation ... one of those acts that only Dmitri Fyodorovitch would be capable of in his anger ... and in his passions! I can’t even describe it.... I can’t find the words. I’ve made inquiries about his victim, and I find he is a very poor man. His name is Snegiryov. He did something wrong in the army and was discharged. I can’t tell you what. And now he has sunk into terrible poverty, with his family—an unhappy family of sick children and, I believe, an insane wife. He has lived here a long time; he used to work as a copying clerk, but now he’s getting no work at all. I thought that if you ... that is, I thought ... I don’t know. I’m so confused. You see, I wanted to ask you, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, to go to him, to find some excuse to go to them—I mean to that captain—oh, goodness, how badly I explain it!—and delicately, carefully, as only you know how” (Alyosha blushed), “to manage to give him this help, these two hundred roubles. He’ll be sure to take it.... I mean, persuade him to take it.... Or rather, what do I mean? You see, it’s not meant as compensation to stop him from taking legal action (because I believe he intended to), but simply as a token of sympathy, of a wish to help him, from me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s betrothed, not from himself.... But you know.... I would go myself, but you’ll know how to do it so much better. He lives in Lake Street, in the house of a woman called Kalmikov.... For God’s sake, Alexey Fyodorovitch, do this for me, and now ... now I’m rather ... tired. Good-by!”

She turned and vanished behind the portière so quickly that Alyosha had no time to say a word, though he wanted to speak. He longed to beg her pardon, to blame himself, to say something, because his heart was full and he couldn’t bear to leave the room without it. But Madame Hohlakov took him by the hand and drew him along with her. In the hall she stopped him again, as before.

“She’s proud, she’s struggling with herself; but she’s kind, charming, generous,” she exclaimed in a half-whisper. “Oh, how I love her, especially at times, and how glad I am about everything again! Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, you didn’t know, but I must tell you, that we all, all of us—both her aunts, I, everyone, even Lise—have been hoping and praying for nothing else for the last month except that she would give up your favorite Dmitri, who takes no notice of her and doesn’t care for her, and marry Ivan Fyodorovitch—such an excellent and cultivated young man, who loves her more than anything in the world. We’re in a regular plot to bring it about, and I’m even staying on here, perhaps, for that reason.”
“But she was crying—she’s been hurt again,” cried Alyosha.
“Never trust a woman’s tears, Alexey Fyodorovitch. In cases like this I’m never on the side of the women. I’m always on the side of the men.”
“Mamma, you’re spoiling him,” Lise’s little voice called from behind the door.
“No, it was all my fault. I’m horribly to blame,” Alyosha repeated, inconsolable, hiding his face in his hands in an agony of remorse for his thoughtlessness.
“Quite the opposite; you behaved like an angel, like an angel. I’m ready to say so a thousand times over.”
“Mamma, how did he behave like an angel?” Lise’s voice was heard again.
“I suddenly got the idea,” Alyosha went on as though he hadn’t heard Lise, “that she loved Ivan, and so I said that stupid thing.... What will happen now?”
“To whom, to whom?” cried Lise. “Mamma, you really want to be the death of me. I ask you and you don’t answer.”
At that moment the maid ran in.
“Katerina Ivanovna is ill.... She’s crying, struggling ... hysterics.”
“What’s the matter?” cried Lise, in a tone of real anxiety. “Mamma, I’m the one who’ll have hysterics, not her!”

“Lise, for mercy’s sake, don’t scream, don’t hound me. At your age you can’t know everything that grown-up people know. I’ll come and tell you everything you ought to know. Oh, mercy on us! I’m coming, I’m coming.... Hysterics is a good sign, Alexey Fyodorovitch; it’s an excellent thing that she’s hysterical. That’s just as it should be. In such cases I’m always against the woman, against all these feminine tears and hysterics. Run and tell her, Yulia, that I’ll fly to her. As for Ivan Fyodorovitch going away like that, it’s her own fault. But he won’t go away. Lise, for mercy’s sake, don’t scream! Oh, yes; you’re not screaming. It’s I who am screaming. Forgive your mamma; but I’m delighted, delighted, delighted! Did you notice, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how young, how young Ivan Fyodorovitch was just now when he went out, when he said all that and went out? I thought he was so learned, such a _savant_, and all of a sudden he behaved so warmly, so openly and youthfully, with such youthful inexperience, and it was all so fine, like you.... And the way he quoted that German verse, it was just like you! But I must fly, I must fly! Alexey Fyodorovitch, hurry and carry out her errand, and then hurry back. Lise, do you want anything now? For mercy’s sake, don’t keep Alexey Fyodorovitch a minute. He’ll come back to you at once.”
Madame Hohlakov finally ran off. Before leaving, Alyosha was about to open the door to see Lise.
“Absolutely not,” cried Lise. “Not now, absolutely not. Speak through the door. How did you come to be an angel? That’s the only thing I want to know.”
“For a dreadful piece of stupidity, Lise! Good-by!”
“Don’t you dare go away like that!” Lise began.
“Lise, I have a real sorrow! I’ll be back right away, but I have a great, great sorrow!”
And he ran out of the room.
